# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm's Comment on the Halden Pilot

Sections 1–5 are a useful re-analysis. Several of their points match the critique of the Halden paper above: the mechanical per-hour metric, the overstated scheduled-hours denominator, the nominal revenue figure, and the sectoral overclaim. They add genuinely new evidence from the microdata on attrition, output records and actual hours.

The conclusion, however, makes the same kind of error the comment criticises in Halden: it claims more than its data show. Sections 6–8 replace evidence with argument, and they read the Varden trial selectively.

I checked the arithmetic:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Table 2 gains: 95.1/0.8, 98.4/0.859, 95.4/0.861 | +18.9%, +14.6%, +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours ratios: 34.6/40.3 and 34.8/40.4 | 0.859 and 0.861 ✓ |
| Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |

Two figures do not check out (points 3 and 5 below).

## Major issues

**1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own results.**
- The abstract says the four problems account for "most" of the gain.
- After the corrections, a +10.8% gain remains.
- The conclusion then calls the gains "entirely an artifact."

Only novelty is offered to close that gap, and novelty is argued for, not measured (point 4). The Data note also says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. The defensible conclusion is that the Halden gain shrinks by more than half under the available corrections, and that the remainder is of uncertain durability.

**2. The Varden trial is cited selectively.**
- The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature."
- It ignores the same trial's case-processing stratum. That stratum meets every standard the comment recommends: randomisation, a control group, administrative output, timesheet hours and no attrition problem. It found a +12.5% gain per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months.
- That result is close to the comment's own corrected +10.8%. It also directly contradicts "entirely an artifact of measurement [and] selection."

Novelty cannot be excluded at nine months. But Varden's control offices also knew a trial was running, which partly addresses the "under evaluation" version of the novelty argument. The comment needs to engage with this stratum, not leave it out.

**3. Table 2 compares different subsets, so it does not isolate the corrections.**
The four rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The steps from row to row mix the effect of each correction with changes in which organisations are included. Compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations, so each correction's effect is clean. Also report the manager index for the 23 and the 17. The 23's manager index (98.9) is close to the full sample's 98.7. That is mildly reassuring on representativeness, and worth saying.

**4. The novelty argument is not evidence, and the direct test is available but unused.**
- *Energy is not output.* A decline in self-reported energy does not show that productivity is declining.
- *The extrapolation is wrong on its own terms.* A linear line from 0.61 at month 3 to 0.29 at month 6 reaches zero at about month 8.7, not month 10. A two-point straight-line extrapolation of a series that rose from 0 to its peak is not meaningful anyway.
- *The direct test exists.* Halden collected the output index monthly, and the comment has the microdata. If per-hour output declined over months 1–6, show it. If it did not, the novelty claim is weakened. Leaving this out is the comment's largest gap.
- *The burden of proof is not one-sided.* "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a rhetorical move. Durability is unknown in both directions.

**5. The hours breakdown does not add up.**
Logged extra time is +0.7 hours a day on four days (2.8 hours) plus 1.6 hours on the day off. That is 4.4 hours above the 32 scheduled, or about 36.4 hours. The reported average is 34.6, which implies only about 2.6 extra hours, or roughly +0.25 hours a day if the 1.6 is right. Either a figure is wrong, or the averages are taken over different bases (for example, only staff who worked the day off). Please reconcile them.

**6. Attrition is documented but not quantified.**
The finding that seven of the nine withdrew *after* the schedule began, mostly citing workload, is important. It contradicts the working paper's description and deserves prominence. Still:
- the conclusion lists attrition among the problems that "account for" the gain, without estimating its effect;
- bounds would help, such as intention-to-treat estimates under stated assumptions about the withdrawn organisations' output, or Lee-type bounds;
- exit reasons cover only 8 of the 9 organisations, and the ninth should be noted.

## Further points on the output and revenue corrections

- **"Billable hours delivered" is an input, not an output.** For organisations that use it, a cut in hours lowers measured output almost automatically. Output per actual hour then becomes largely a utilisation rate. Say how many of the 23 used it, and show the results without them.
- **Records are not necessarily the truth.** Managers may have counted dimensions of output that the records miss. The abstract's wording ("overstates output relative to organisations' own records") is accurate. The conclusion's "overstated output by roughly four points" is stronger than that. Use the abstract's wording throughout. Also report the paired test: 19 of 23 in one direction gives p ≈ 0.003 on a sign test.
- **CPI is a rough deflator.** Non-profits' grant income and business-to-business prices do not track consumer prices. Name the country and price index, or present the figure as approximate. Note too that it covers only 52 organisations.

## Section 7 misrepresents the Varden authors

- **They did not claim a mechanism.** The Varden authors flagged the analysis as unregistered, said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's critique agrees with their own caveats, but is written as if they had overclaimed.
- **The offices were not a post hoc subgroup.** The seven offices are the entire pre-registered treated case-processing stratum.
- **The data were not chosen after the results were known.** They were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **The randomised comparison is omitted.** Varden also reports a 3.3-hour treated-versus-control difference in meeting time, which is better evidence than the seven-office correlation.
- **There is an unacknowledged tension.** If meetings were confirmed as a mechanism, that would be a lasting, non-novelty source of gains. The section reads as dismissing the one candidate that would contradict the "entirely novelty" conclusion.

A fair version: "Interesting and plausible, currently unconfirmed; the registered 24-month test will be informative."

## Smaller points

- **Retail.** The three retail organisations with records (−11.2%) are a very small sample. They are fine as an illustration but should not carry inferential weight.
- **Recommendations.** The section-8 recommendations are good. Add same-subset decompositions and month-by-month output trajectories, which the comment itself should model.

## Overall

Keep sections 1–5, with the fixes above. In section 6, replace the argument with the monthly-output analysis. Rewrite section 7 to represent Varden accurately. Revise the conclusion along these lines:

> "Under the corrections possible, the Halden per-hour gain falls from 23.4% to about 11% in the subset with usable data; attrition likely biases it further upward by an unquantified amount. Randomised evidence (Varden) shows a gain of similar size in non-coverage-bound work and a loss of output in coverage-bound work. Whether per-hour gains persist beyond the first year is unknown."

I can draft the revised conclusion, a same-subset version of Table 2, or a specification for the monthly trajectory analysis.
